turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: Fix the handoff first. Then buy the tool. I call the reverse order expensive confusion.

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: In one team I advised, nobody owned the next step after a sales call. We named an owner. I don't have a number for the improvement.

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: I used to arrive with this enormous checklist. Honestly, I was so busy asking my questions that I missed what the client was telling me. Now I leave a little room for the unexpected.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: So all consultants should abandon checklists?

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: No, I wouldn't go that far. A checklist helps. Just don't let it do the listening for you.

required_phrases: don't let it do the listening

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: I separate queue time from processing time. A faster processing step doesn't necessarily reduce end-to-end latency when the queue dominates.

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: As a hypothetical example, imagine 10 minutes of processing and 2 days in a queue. That is an illustration, not a result from a client engagement.

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: A handoff is a relay, not a parcel drop. You need to know the next person has the baton. Sending an email is not the same as transferring responsibility.

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: My practical test is simple: ask both people who owns the next step. If they give different answers, you've found the gap.

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: I tend to start small. That isn't always right, especially when the system is already failing. But in my experience, a small experiment often makes disagreement more concrete.

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: Earlier I said a month. Let me correct that: I mean a short trial, not a fixed duration. The team needs to define that.

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: For me, a decision needs a home. If everybody owns it, sometimes nobody carries it. I ask who will carry this decision tomorrow, when the meeting is finished.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Could we say this doubles productivity?

turns.speaker: participant
turns.text: No, I cannot say that. I only know it makes the responsibility clearer.
